Boule or Baguette?
A Study on Task Topology, Length Generalization,
and the Benefit of Reasoning Traces

William L. Tong Affiliation: School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University Affiliation: Kempner Institute for the Study of Artificial and Natural Intelligence, Harvard University    Ege Çakar Affiliation: School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University Affiliation: Kempner Institute for the Study of Artificial and Natural Intelligence, Harvard University    Cengiz Pehlevan Affiliation: School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University Affiliation: Kempner Institute for the Study of Artificial and Natural Intelligence, Harvard University Affiliation: Center for Brain Sciences, Harvard University Correspondence to: wtong@g.harvard.edu
Abstract

Recent years have witnessed meteoric progress in reasoning models: neural networks that generate intermediate reasoning traces (RTs) before producing a final output. Despite the rapid advancement, our understanding of how RTs support reasoning, and the limits of this paradigm, remain incomplete. To promote greater clarity, we introduce PITA: a novel large-scale dataset of over 23 million statements in propositional logic and their corresponding proofs. As a benchmark for robust reasoning, we focus on length generalization: if a model is trained to determine truth or falsity on statements with proofs up to fixed length, how well does it generalize to statements requiring longer proofs? We propose notions of (1) task depth and (2) task breadth, which measure respectively (1) the number of steps required to solve an example from a task and (2) the number of unique examples across a task. We vary these quantities across subsets of PITA, and find that RT models generalize well on broad and shallow subsets, while deteriorating on narrow and deep subsets relative to non-RT baselines. To determine whether our results are idiosyncratic to PITA or indicative of general phenomena, we compare our results to a simple synthetic task based on syllogisms. Our resulting theory suggests fundamental scalings that limit how well RT models perform on deep tasks, and highlights their generalization strengths on broad tasks. Our findings overall identify fundamental benefits and limitations inherent in using reasoning traces.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

In just a few short years, neural networks equipped with reasoning traces (RTs) have attained top performance at international math competitions (Luong & Lockhart, 2025; Chervonyi et al., 2025), threatened to displace software engineers (Jimenez et al., 2023; Belzner et al., 2023; Eloundou et al., 2023), saturated dozens of benchmarks designed to measure human-level reasoning (Achiam et al., 2023; Team et al., 2023; Deveci & Ataman, 2025), and accomplished among many more astonishing feats big and small (Chu et al., 2024). And yet, despite the clear empirical success of these methods, debate abounds regarding how and why reasoning traces improve performance. Perhaps RTs allow a model to decompose a difficult problem into simpler steps (Wei et al., 2022) or allow the model to catch errors and backtrack (Guo et al., 2025). At the same time, others have observed that the content of generated reasoning traces are not always relevant to solving the task (Turpin et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Yee et al., 2024), reasoning models are highly susceptible to distribution shifts (Zhao et al., 2025; Stechly et al., 2024), and in some cases, less reasoning paradoxically appears to be better (Wu et al., 2025). With growing awareness around the surprising and sometimes dangerous limitations of reasoning models (Song et al., 2025), combined with the rapid introduction of this technology across mainstream products, it is more important than ever to understand the fundamental benefits and weaknesses of this paradigm.

To this end, we introduce PITA: a large-scale propositional inference task consisting of over 23 million statements and 95 billion tokens in propositional logic11 1 Our dataset is available on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/datasets/williamtong105/pita.. As the logical core of mathematics, propositional logic is a representative and tractable microcosm of general reasoning. To ensure rigor and avoid confounds associated with natural language, we formalize our dataset in Lean (De Moura et al., 2015). For each statement in PITA, a model must determine whether the statement is true or false. The corresponding proof presents a natural and canonical reasoning trace determining the statement’s veracity. We compare RT models that are trained using proofs against direct prediction (DP) models, which are not provided proofs. To test the robustness of reasoning, we evaluate length generalization: models are trained on statements with proofs up to a fixed length, then tested on statements with longer proofs. We illustrate PITA in Figure 1.

In PITA, we define task depth and task breadth, which relate to the task’s topology. Depth measures the number of steps required to prove a statement. Breadth measures the number of unique statements for a given size, where size is determined by the number of propositional atoms. These measures may generalize to any reasoning task, where depth relates to the number of reasoning steps required to solve a task and breadth relates to the size of the task space.

We divide PITA into several splits with varying depth and breadth, and find that RT models generalize most effectively on broad and shallow splits (“boule”-shaped), while deteriorating on narrow and deep splits (“baguette”-shaped) relative to direct prediction models. Given that RTs are presumed to benefit most on tasks with step-wise structure (Nye et al., 2021; Prystawski et al., 2023), it is particularly surprising that an RT model underperforms the DP baseline on deep splits.

To determine whether these outcomes are idiosyncratic to PITA, or indicative of a broader phenomenon, we compare our results to a simpler task based on transitive inference (TI), the process of reasoning about syllogisms. TI reflects the step-wise reasoning of propositional logic while being more tractable to study, offering a grounded perspective on task topology and reasoning traces. Using arguments based on margin maximization in neural networks (Chizat & Bach, 2020; Morwani et al., 2023), we explain empirically observed scalings that relate task breadth, depth, and model width, revealing both the generalization strengths of RT for broad tasks, and fundamental limitations for deep tasks. These theoretical results suggest fundamental benefits and limitations inherent in using RTs for reasoning tasks with syllogism structure.

1.1 Related work

Reasoning traces entered mainstream practice with the introduction of chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting (Wei et al., 2022; Nye et al., 2021). Originally, CoT was an inference-time technique where a language model is prompted to “think step-by-step,” producing a reasoning trace that guides it towards the correct answer. It has since grown to encompass a wide diversity of both inference- and training-time interventions that equip a neural network with some capacity to use or generate reasoning traces (Chu et al., 2024). In common use, RT and CoT are almost synonymous, but in this study we prefer “RT” to avoid the connotation of inference-time prompting.

A number of theoretical studies have sought to explain how RTs benefit neural networks. Allowing a Transformer to generate intermediate tokens increases its expressivity, an advantage that can be described precisely using circuit complexity theory (Feng et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Merrill & Sabharwal, 2023). Others have observed that reasoning traces confer statistical advantages when learning tasks that would otherwise require a large number of training examples or large model size (Abbe et al., 2024; Kim & Suzuki, 2024; Hu et al., 2024; Wies et al., 2022). Generating RTs may also be interpreted as a form of search, enabling the model to more effectively explore the task space (Kim et al., 2025; Gandhi et al., 2024; Prystawski et al., 2023).

RTs are also thought to benefit length generalization (Huang et al., 2025; Ahuja & Mansouri, 2024; Xiao & Liu, 2024; Anil et al., 2022). In general, length generalization is challenging for Transformer models, and depends highly on training procedure and architectural choices like positional encodings (Zhou et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024; Kazemnejad et al., 2023). Transformers also struggle with very large input contexts (Kuratov et al., 2024; Hsieh et al., 2024; Roberts et al., 2024; Tay et al., 2020), potentially hindering their ability to generalize when tasks require long reasoning traces. Indeed, recent evidence suggests that prolonged reasoning traces can be harmful (Wu et al., 2025; Hassid et al., 2025; Ghosal et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025). We continue this discussion by connecting length generalization with task topology, clarifying cases where RTs benefit or harm.

Our tasks focus specifically on propositional logic and transitive inference, domains that probe the model’s capacity to handle syllogisms. Logical reasoning has been studied across many settings in both natural language (Saparov & He, 2022; Tafjord et al., 2021; Clark et al., 2020; Han et al., 2024) and formal language (Pan et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2024; An et al., 2024). A number of works have compared logical reasoning to graph operations (Abbe et al., 2024; Minegishi et al., 2025; Sanford et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Prystawski et al., 2023). Related to our work, Abbe et al. (2024) formalize syllogism as an in-context graph connectivity task, finding that CoT interventions may enable greater learning efficiency. Minegishi et al. (2025) interpret the reasoning process as graph traversal. Using clustering techniques to extract graphs from hidden representations, they identify correlations between topological properties of the graph and the models’ performance. We continue this analogy between logical reasoning and graph operations, with a focus on properties of the task-induced graph that support or hinder length generalization.

Transitive inference (TI) is a specific case of graph-based approaches to reasoning. A classic cognitive task in humans and animals (Piaget, 1928; Call et al., 2017), TI presents a set of stimuli together with an ordering relation. During training, the subject observes pairwise relations between stimuli. At test time, the subject must transitively infer the correct relation between unobserved pairs. TI is a well established test for syllogism reasoning in psychology (Vasconcelos, 2008; Call et al., 2017), and witnessing increasing application to neural networks (Lippl et al., 2024; Kay et al., 2024; Geerts et al., 2025). We build on this tradition by employing TI as a tractable yet phenomenologically rich setting for measuring reasoning in complex models.

2 PITA: a propositional inference task

We introduce PITA: a large-scale synthetic dataset of propositional logic, formalized in Lean. To the best of our knowledge, PITA is the largest dataset of Lean theorems to date, with over 23 million statements and 95 billion tokens. The data-generating procedure for PITA is unbounded, allowing for as many additional statements as compute permits. We leverage PITA to evaluate logical reasoning in LLMs at scale, uncovering surprising generalization differences between RT models and direct prediction baselines.

Figure 1 illustrates the format of PITA. The dataset consists of four splits based on syntactic families of propositions, described in more detail below. To construct an example, we enumerate or sample a statement under the appropriate syntactic constraints, then construct a proof using a focused proof search procedure (Liang & Miller, 2009; An et al., 2024). The proof is then translated into Lean code, wrapped in our XML template, and tokenized. For a brief primer on propositional logic and proof systems, see Appendix A.

2.1 PITA splits

We organize PITA into four dataset splits, with varying topology determined by the underlying reasoning process. The two metrics we use to describe topology are task depth and task breadth. Depth measures the number of steps required to prove a statement in a split, counted as the number of unique proof states between the statement and final classification. This count includes proofs states added by backtrack demonstrations. Doing so more accurately reflects the real volume of computation required to prove a statement, as compared to an idealized measure based on the shortest path (which is unknown at the start). Breadth measures the number of unique statements for a given size, where size is counted by the number of atoms in the statement. For example, consider the Imply split, which consists of statements that have only the implication (→\rightarrow) connective. For a size of 2 atoms, the breadth of Imply is 6: p→qp\rightarrow q, p→pp\rightarrow p, ⊤→⊤\top\rightarrow\top, ⊤→⊥\top\rightarrow\bot, ⊥→⊤\bot\rightarrow\top, and ⊥→⊥\bot\rightarrow\bot. 22 2 When counting statements, we do not count differences in variable names. Hence, p→qp\rightarrow q and q→pq\rightarrow p and p′→q′p^{\prime}\rightarrow q^{\prime} are all the same, but p→pp\rightarrow p is distinct. This choice reflects an invariance of propositional logic: a statement’s truth value cannot be changed by changing variable names. Further, including variable names would allow the breadth of any split to be artificially modified by introducing or removing names, reducing its descriptive utility for differentiating model performance. Avoiding variable names contributes to a consistent baseline for measuring breadth across all splits. For similar reasons, with commutative and associative connectives (∨\vee and ∧\wedge), we ignore differences in permutation and association. Hence, p∨(q∨r)p\vee(q\vee r) is the same as (q∨p)∨r(q\vee p)\vee r.

Depth and breadth correspond to natural descriptions of topology in general problem-solving tasks. Depth relates to the number of steps required to solve a task. Breadth relates to the size of the task space. These are general and intuitive properties of any task with step-wise structure, and historically studied in great depth for classic search and planning algorithms in AI (Russell & Norvig, 2016). We anticipate that our intuitions remain valid in many tasks beyond PITA.

We investigate how task topology influences length generalization in reasoning trace models, compared against direct prediction baselines. We construct four dataset splits delineating different subsets of propositional logic, with varying depth and breadth:

  • •

    Full. The full space of propositional statements with no restrictions. This split is the broadest.

  • •

    Imply. The implicational fragment of propositional logic: only implication-connectives are permitted. Implication is functionally complete (Enderton, 2001): every proposition in Full can also be expressed in Imply. Together with Full, these splits are the broadest.

  • •

    Or. Statements that have a single imply connective, a single variable in the antecedent, and only or-connectives in the consequent. Propositions of this form are equivalent to a membership check: does the variable in the antecedent occur in the consequent? This split is the narrowest.

  • •

    PHP. The Pigeonhole Principle (PHP) states that given mm pigeons and nn holes, if m>nm>n, then at least one hole contains two or more pigeons (see Eq (8) for the exact statement in propositional logic). We use a harder variation in which pigeons are constrained to occupy subsets of available holes. These propositions require proofs that can be exponentially long in the number of pigeons and holes (Razborov, 2001), so they are often employed to stress-test proof systems (Haken, 1985; Balsiger et al., 2000). This split is the deepest. Together with Or, these splits are the narrowest.

We plot the depths and breadths of each split in Figure 1. Full and Imply are boule-shaped splits, significantly broader and generally shallower than the other two. Or and PHP are baguette-shaped splits, substantially narrower than the first two, with PHP notably deeper than any other split.

A task becomes more difficult as it deepens and broadens. Our boule-shaped splits highlight the impact of breadth, testing how models handle an increasing diversity of examples. Our baguette-shaped splits highlight the impact depth, testing how models handle an increasing number of reasoning steps. See Appendix C for example propositions in each split, along with additional details on their construction.

2.2 Model

We test Qwen2.5-Coder, Gemma 3, and Llama 3 on PITA, across many sizes. We start with pretrained models, and finetune on PITA.

Input formats for our RT and DP models are illustrated in Figure 1. For each statement in PITA, the model determines whether the statement is true or false. Each statement also has a corresponding proof establishing its veracity or falsity. RT models are trained on statements with proofs before rendering their final classification. DP models are trained only on statements, and output a classification directly without proof. In this way, we employ proofs as a natural, canonical reasoning trace, reflecting the role of proofs in math to establish the veracity of theorems. Our setting is similar to cases where models are trained directly on datasets that embed reasoning traces, where RTs are hand-constructed (Ye et al., 2025), generated by large reasoning models (Guha et al., 2025), or (as in our case) constructed from a verifiable source (Yang et al., 2023). All models are finetuned on next-token prediction with cross-entropy loss, using QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023). All hyperparameter configurations and implementation details are listed in Appendix C.

We evaluate models by their ability for length generalization: models are trained on statements with proofs up to the median proof length of the split, and evaluated on statements with longer proofs. During evaluation, the model generates tokens autoregressively until producing a special classification token indicating whether the statement is true or false. By virtue of their training, DP models almost always produce a classification token immediately, whereas RT models generate an intermediate proof first. Since our focus is on studying the impact of reasoning traces, rather than the model’s ability to generate correct proofs, we ignore the content of the reasoning trace and measure accuracy only from the classification token33 3 An informal inspection of the generated reasoning traces indicates that models generally produce plausible proofs that are very similar to the ground truth. We offer a few examples in Appendix E, and defer a more thorough examination of LLM-generated proofs for future work.. If a model fails to produce a classification token within the max context length, the test point is marked as an error.

2.3 Experimental results

Figure 2 plots the generalization accuracy of RT and DP models across the Qwen 2.5 Coder family. Additional plots for Gemma 3 and Llama 3 are provided in Appendix D. Reasoning trace models tend to outperform their direct prediction counterparts on the breadth-dominated boule-shaped splits Full and Imply, particularly for larger models. The reverse is true for the depth-dominated baguette-shaped splits, where DP models outperform RT models by as much as 50 percentage points on PHP for the 7B model. The same trends hold consistently across all other model families.

These results indicate a prevalent reversal in the generalization gap between RT and DP models on breadth-dominated tasks versus depth-dominated tasks. One intuitive explanation for this outcome is that long reasoning traces sometimes hurt model performance. Because deeper tasks require more steps to solve, they also require a longer reasoning trace. Recent findings suggest that long RTs incur a number of significant issues: long generation may introduce cascading errors (Bengio et al., 2015), autoregressive prompting is susceptible to an exposure bias (Schmidt, 2019), Transformers have difficulty processing long contexts (Kuratov et al., 2024), and empirical performance sometimes correlates negatively with reasoning trace length (Wu et al., 2025). This outcome is consistent with the emerging narrative that long RTs hurt performance. Indeed, a detailed error breakdown of an example RT model (Figure 10) suggests that failure to terminate accounts for a large proportion of RT errors.

However, this explanation glosses over the many arguments suggesting that RTs are helpful precisely for tasks with salient step-wise structure (Nye et al., 2021). Indeed, Figure 10 suggests RT models commit fewer false positive and false negative errors generally. In these settings, direct prediction models are shown to either learn a short-cut solution that generalizes poorly (Liu et al., 2022), or fail to learn a solution at all within a reasonable training budget (Feng et al., 2023; Abbe et al., 2024). This literature would suggest RT models should always outperform DP models on tasks like PITA, regardless of task topology. Perhaps RT model performance would fall on deep splits due to the issue listed above, but should not DP model performance fall even further?

It remains unclear how this tradeoff operates between and long-trace failures and generalization strengths, and whether these results are idiosyncratic to PITA or indicative of broader phenomena. To provide a point of comparison, we next consider a simple task that models the essential skill underlying propositional logic — transitive inference — and reproduces these trends in a minimal, tractable setting. Our theoretical analysis offers additional insight on fundamental tradeoffs inherent to RT methods.

3 Transitive inference

Transitive inference (TI) has as long, rich history in developmental and comparative psychology, where it is frequently employed to describe the ability to reason with syllogisms (Piaget, 1928). Given the facts “A implies B” and “B implies C,” a subject may transitively infer that “A implies C.” TI is also witnessing increasing application in neural networks to measure reasoning (Lippl et al., 2024; Kay et al., 2024; Geerts et al., 2025).

Syllogisms are a fundamental component of propositional logic, and indeed of logical reasoning generally. TI presents a salient and phenomenologically rich foundation to more deeply explore logical reasoning in neural networks. In the remainder of this paper, we present an analysis of TI in Transformers that connects task topology to generalization tradeoffs between RT and DP models, offering a grounded perspective of our results on PITA.

3.1 Task

Our TI task consists of a set of symbols S={si}S=\{s_{i}\} and a set of transitive relations R={si→sj}R=\{s_{i}\rightarrow s_{j}\}. Transitivity requires that if si→sj∈Rs_{i}\rightarrow s_{j}\in R and sj→sk∈Rs_{j}\rightarrow s_{k}\in R, then si→sk∈Rs_{i}\rightarrow s_{k}\in R. The model is then presented pairs si,sjs_{i},s_{j} with label

y={1if​si→sj∈R−1otherwise.y=\begin{cases}1&\quad\text{if}\;s_{i}\rightarrow s_{j}\in R\\ -1&\quad\text{otherwise}\,.\end{cases}

A relation si→sks_{i}\rightarrow s_{k} is derived if there exists one or more intermediate symbols j1,j2,…j_{1},j_{2},\ldots such that si→sj1;sj1→sj2;sj2→…→sks_{i}\rightarrow s_{j_{1}};\,s_{j_{1}}\rightarrow s_{j_{2}};\,s_{j_{2}}\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow s_{k}. If a relation is not derived, it is direct.

To construct a simple analog of task depth and breadth, we consider the following structure of transitive relations. Symbols are organized into BB distinct branches, each consisting of DD symbols. We denote the nnth branch as a set ℬn={s1n,s2n,…,sDn}\mathcal{B}^{n}=\{s_{1}^{n},s_{2}^{n},\ldots,s_{D}^{n}\} with direct relations s1n→s2n;s2n→s3n​…​sD−1n→sDns_{1}^{n}\rightarrow s_{2}^{n};\,s_{2}^{n}\rightarrow s_{3}^{n}\,\ldots\,s_{D-1}^{n}\rightarrow s_{D}^{n}. There do not exist relations between the symbols of two different branches.

To determine whether sim→sjns_{i}^{m}\rightarrow s_{j}^{n} is a valid syllogism, we need to enumerate the intermediate relations sim→si+1m→…→sDms_{i}^{m}\rightarrow s_{i+1}^{m}\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow s_{D}^{m}. If sjn∈{si+1m​…​sDm}s_{j}^{n}\in\{s_{i+1}^{m}\ldots s_{D}^{m}\}, then the relation is valid. Performing this check requires up to DD reasoning steps, so DD naturally parameterizes the task depth. For a fixed depth, the number of branches BB determines the number of possible symbol pairs, and therefore the size of the task space. Hence, BB parameterizes the task breadth.

We evaluate length generalization in the following way. The position along a branch nn may be defined by the number of direct relations leading from the first symbols s1ns_{1}^{n} (which conveniently aligns with our indexing). We denote the distance between two symbols as d⁡(sin,sjn)=|j−i|d(s_{i}^{n},s_{j}^{n})=|j-i|. Since each branch has the same number DD of symbols, we also define distance between symbols of different branches as d⁡(sin,sjm)=|j−i|d(s_{i}^{n},s_{j}^{m})=|j-i|. During training, we present symbol pairs up to a fixed distance kk. During testing, we measure generalization accuracy on symbol pairs with distance greater than kk.

Examples are sampled uniformly at random and presented to the model online. Exactly half of the examples have positive labels, and half have negative. Given a candidate relation sim→sjns_{i}^{m}\rightarrow s_{j}^{n}, a negative example may be constructed either by ensuring m≠nm\neq n or i>ji>j. We concentrate on negative examples where branches differ, finding that this setting is already sufficient to reproduce the generalization characteristics observed in PITA, and defer a more detailed analysis of i>ji>j inverted negative examples for future work. We illustrate our task in Figure 3.

3.2 Model

We study single-layer, single-head, decoder-only Transformer models. Input symbols s1n,s2n,…s_{1}^{n},s_{2}^{n},\ldots are mapped to embeddings 𝐱1n,𝐱2n,…∈ℝH\mathbf{x}_{1}^{n},\mathbf{x}_{2}^{n},\ldots\in\mathbb{R}^{H}, sampled as 𝐱in∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈H)\mathbf{x}_{i}^{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{H}) and fixed throughout training.

Embeddings pass through a self-attention layer. For an input sequence consisting of embeddings 𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱L\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{L}, the LLth activation 𝐯L\mathbf{v}_{L} is given by

𝐯L=𝐕⁡(a1​L​𝐱1+a2​L​𝐱2+…+aL​L​𝐱L),\mathbf{v}_{L}=\mathbf{V}\left(a_{1L}\,\mathbf{x}_{1}+a_{2L}\,\mathbf{x}_{2}+\ldots+a_{LL}\,\mathbf{x}_{L}\right)\,,

where attention weights are given by

ai​L=softmax​(1H​𝐱i⊺​𝐊⊺​𝐐​𝐱L).a_{iL}=\text{softmax}\left(\frac{1}{H}\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\intercal}\mathbf{K}^{\intercal}\mathbf{Q}\,\mathbf{x}_{L}\right)\,.

As usual, the softmax is computed across all weights a(⋅)​La_{(\cdot)L} such that ∑iai​L=1\sum_{i}a_{iL}=1. Note, we use the μ\muP scaling prefactor 1/H1/H rather than the original 1/H1/\sqrt{H} (Yang et al., 2022; Bordelon et al., 2024). Weight matrices 𝐊,𝐐,𝐕∈ℝH×H\mathbf{K},\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times H} are initialized in μ\muP.

Activations then pass through an MLP. The LLth logit yLy_{L} is given by

yL=𝐰r⊺​ϕ​(𝐖1​𝐯L).y_{L}=\mathbf{w}_{r}^{\intercal}\phi(\mathbf{W}_{1}\mathbf{v}_{L})\,. (1)

Weight matrices 𝐖1∈ℝH×H,𝐰r∈ℝH\mathbf{W}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times H},\mathbf{w}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{H} are again initialized in μ\muP.

Our essential phenomenology is captured by this minimal model. For simplicity, we omit residual connections, layer normalization, dropout, and biases. We also omit positional encodings. Consistent with (Kazemnejad et al., 2023), we find that model performance remains the same or improves when positional encodings are omitted.

3.2.1 Input format

For the direct prediction model, input pairs are provided directly and a classification is immediately required. Given embeddings 𝐱im\mathbf{x}_{i}^{m} and 𝐱jn\mathbf{x}_{j}^{n}, the input is formatted as

(𝐱im𝐱jn),\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{x}_{i}^{m}&\mathbf{x}_{j}^{n}\end{pmatrix}\,,

producing an input in ℝH×2\mathbb{R}^{H\times 2}  . Using the output logit y2y_{2}, the model is trained using gradient descent on binary cross entropy loss.

For the reasoning trace model, inputs 𝐱im,𝐱jn\mathbf{x}_{i}^{m},\,\mathbf{x}_{j}^{n} are followed by a reasoning trace that enumerates all symbols in the nnth branch. Once the enumeration completes, the model generates a special classification token, denoted here as “✓” if the relation is valid and “×\times” if the relation is invalid. For example,

(𝐱im𝐱jn𝐱1n⋯𝐱j−1n𝐱j+1n⋯𝐱Dn✓).\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{x}_{i}^{m}&\mathbf{x}_{j}^{n}&\mathbf{x}_{1}^{n}&\cdots&\mathbf{x}_{j-1}^{n}&\mathbf{x}_{j+1}^{n}\cdots\mathbf{x}_{D}^{n}&\checkmark\end{pmatrix}\,.

This input produces an embedding in ℝH×(D+2)\mathbb{R}^{H\times(D+2)}. There are other reasonable input schemes, like terminating early if 𝐱im\mathbf{x}_{i}^{m} is recovered in the reasoning trace. The format we choose simplifies our theoretical analysis, and also performs very well for the RT model in practice (Figure 11). The model is trained on autoregressive next-token prediction using gradient descent on cross entropy loss. All hyperparameters and setup details are listed in Appendix C.

3.3 TI results

We identify empirical scalings that relate generalization accuracy with task topology. We also characterize scalings between topology and model width required to maintain high training accuracy. These scalings are summarized in Table 1, and plotted in Figure 3.

To explore where these scalings originate, we conduct a theoretical analysis based on max-margin considerations. Neural networks trained on a classification objective often converge to a set of weights that maximize the margin over their training data (Soudry et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2019). We characterize the max margin solution for our task, in the process identifying constraints that model weights must satisfy to solve transitive inference. These constraints limit the largest task depth DD and breadth BB that a model can learn, as a function of its hidden width HH. We also use these constraints to infer the models’ generalization properties. Our analysis reproduces our empirical scalings, and is detailed in Appendix B.

These results echo our findings on PITA. Reasoning trace models perform better on breadth-dominated boule-shaped tasks: as breadth increases, generalization in the RT model remains unchanged while generalization accuracy in the DP model decays. On the other hand, direct prediction models perform better on depth-dominated baguette-shaped tasks: the depth necessary to maintain high accuracy scales faster with hidden width in DP models compared to RT models.

Our theoretical analysis suggests that the generalization differences between DP and RT models may be understood through a difference in inductive bias. By enumerating over intermediate symbols, the RT model benefits from an inductive bias for a solution that transfers directly from train to test examples (Proposition B.4). As a result, when training accuracy is high, generalization is perfect.

Meanwhile, generalization performance decays in the DP model as breadth increases. We find that the DP model overfits to the training distribution (Section B.4), an effect exacerbated by increasing BB. This outcome resonates with the current understanding that Transformers tend to discover “short-cut” solutions that approximate correct outputs with brittle heuristics (Liu et al., 2022). Although both DP and RT models attain a fast B∝H2B\propto H^{2} scaling in training accuracy, the superior generalization performance of reasoning trace models for large breadth differentiates their strength in a breadth-dominated setting.

When increasing task depth, the DP scaling D∝HD\propto H is notably faster than the RT scaling D∝HD\propto\sqrt{H}. We ultimately trace the slower RT scaling to an issue with processing long-contexts: as depth increases, the reasoning trace also lengthens, making it more difficult to discern the correct label (Proposition B.3). If breadth is small, the DP model may attain high generalization accuracy. Thus, direct prediction outperform reasoning traces on baguette-shaped tasks that are deep and narrow.

Implications for PITA.

Our transitive inference task is substantially simpler than PITA, and different mechanisms may drive the topology/RT relationships we observe in these two settings. Nonetheless, the TI task indicates that our observations generalize to settings beyond PITA, and common intuitions may transfer. Reasoning traces may narrow the gap between train and test propositions, improving generalization. Direct prediction may be prone to spurious signals in the training set, particular when the set of propositions broadens and becomes more complex, reducing generalization performance on breadth-dominated splits. Deep PITA splits necessitate longer proofs, introducing long-context issues that likely handicap generalization in the RT model. Our analysis with TI highlights the particular issue that long contexts are statistically more difficult to process when the relevant signal is weakly dispersed in the total input. On the other hand, DP models benefit from narrower tasks and avoid the pitfalls of long contexts, preserving their length generalization performance on baguette-shaped splits.

4 Discussion

We introduced PITA, a large-scale dataset of statements in propositional logic. We defined two metrics that describe task topology: (1) depth, the number of steps require to solve a task, and (2) breadth, the number of unique examples across a task. Across several model families and sizes, we identified a persistent reversal in length generalization performance between reasoning trace and direct prediction models, where RT models performed well on boule-shaped tasks, and DP models excelled on baguette-shaped tasks.

To explore these trends further, we proposed a transitive inference task that exhibits the same phenomena. Our theoretical analysis suggests that DP models discover suboptimal minima that generalize poorly for increasing task breadth. Reasoning traces narrow the generalization gap, supporting high accuracy for shallow tasks as breadth increases. However, long context hinder RT performance on deep tasks, pulling it below DP models when the task remains narrow.

The surprising performance of DP models indicates a need for more nuance when using RTs. Past work have observed that reasoning traces are minimally beneficial (and occasionally harmful) in domains like text classification and commonsense reasoning (Sprague et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024). Even in propositional logic, a setting that should complement the advantages of reasoning traces, we identify a consistent generalization difference between RT and DP models related to task topology. Our notions of task depth and breadth are general, and we anticipate future work characterizing topology more precisely and across a wider range of settings to predict where direct prediction may excel.

In many domains, the task is both very broad and very deep. For these especially challenging reasoning tasks, it is likely more feasible to improve long-context processing in an RT model than to endow a DP model with magically better generalization. Our results support the growing realization that Transformers perform poorly with long-contexts, and alternative methods are needed. Besides issues with autoregressive generation, our theory on TI additionally highlights the statistical difficulty in processing a long context where the signal is weakly dispersed across many relevant tokens. As reasoning trace techniques grow increasingly popular, we highlight long-context reasoning as an important obstacle hindering current Transformer-based paradigms.

With the general increasing interest in formal reasoning, we add PITA to the growing collection of testbeds for promoting and evaluating logical reasoning in neural networks. As a large-scale, extensible framework for generating Lean-formalized statements in propositional logic, PITA presents many additional opportunities for rigorously testing and developing new models. We look forward to many more frumentaceous findings to come.

Appendix A Primer on propositional logic and proof systems

Propositional logic is a calculus of truth. Given propositions with intrinsic truth value and connectives that join them, propositional logic studies the ultimate truth of their combination. This appendix offers a brief primer to provide some background for our PITA dataset. This topic is deep and nuanced; for a more in-depth treatment of this topic, we recommend Enderton (2001).

A statement in propositional logic (or simply, a proposition) consists of atoms and connectives. An atom is a symbol that denotes truth (⊤\top), falsity (⊥\bot), or a variable (e.g. p,q,r,…p,q,r,\ldots). A connective is a function that takes two propositions and returns a corresponding truth assignment. For instance, the connective and (∧\wedge) evaluates to true only if both inputs are true. Hence, ⊤∧⊤\top\wedge\top is true but ⊤∧⊥\top\wedge\bot is false. Other common connectives are or (∨\vee) and imply (→\rightarrow). The truth assignment of each connective we use in PITA is summarized below in Table 2

We say that a proposition is true if it is a tautology: the proposition remains true for every possible truth/falsity assignment of its variables. Otherwise if the proposition is not a tautology, then we say the proposition is false. To demonstrate whether a propositional statement is true, one may simply enumerate over all possible truth assignments and verify that the statement remains true. However, this approach requires 2n2^{n} evaluations for a statement with nn variables, which becomes impractical for large propositions. To demonstrate truth more efficiently, we may instead construct a proof.

A.1 Proofs and proof search

A proof is a sequence of transformations that converts a proposition into other (usually simpler) propositions while preserving tautology. These transformations are called inference rules. For example, a common inference rule is modus ponens (MP), which requires two propositions as input: a proposition pp, and a proposition p→qp\rightarrow q. MP then allows us to transform these two propositions into the single proposition qq.

There are a variety of valid inference rules beyond MP, and different proof systems permit different sets of inference rules. In PITA, we use rules of natural deduction, which are a common choice with desirable properties for both reasoning about proofs and engineering automated proof search procedures. For a more detailed discussion of natural deduction and examples of its inference rules, see Pelletier & Hazen (2021).

Armed with inference rules, the process of constructing a proof can be thought of as the process of identifying the correct sequence of rules that translates the starting proposition into the proposition ⊤\top. Under this interpretation, inference rules induce a graph-like topology: sets of propositions are nodes, and inference rules are directed edges that connect them. If a path exists from a proposition pp to the the proposition ⊤\top, then pp must be true. Otherwise if no such path exists, pp must be false44 4 Since inference rules may introduce additional propositions that need to be concurrently proved, proofs technically constitute trees through this graph rather than paths. A proof is true if all leaves of this tree terminate in ⊤\top. Otherwise, the proof is false. In this discussion, we have also ignored nuances related to syntactic truth versus semantic truth, and falsity versus unprovability. These issues are important but not immediately relevant in our setting. For additional discussion on these topics and more, we recommend Enderton (2001).

In this way, proving a proposition reduces to implementing a search procedure over the graph of propositional statements and inference rules. Common approaches to performing this search procedure are sensitive to symmetries inherent to the different logical connectives, and apply inference rules in deliberate order to control the size of the search space. To construct the proofs used in PITA, we employ an algorithm from the family of methods called focused proof search (Liang & Miller, 2009), a popular choice for constructing efficient and intuitive proofs to arbitrary propositional statements.

Appendix B Theoretical analysis of transitive inference

In this appendix, we detail our analysis of a Transformer learning the transitive inference task, introduced in Section 3. Our analysis is organized in three stages.

  1. 1.

    We begin by simplifying our Transformer model further. We argue that attention becomes uniform over inputs for our task, reducing our model to a two-layer MLP. Building on (Tong & Pehlevan, 2025), we introduce a sample-coordinate representation of our model weights, in which we characterize our weights in the span of training samples.

  2. 2.

    We identify the set of weights that maximize the classification margin in our transitive inference task. Because neural networks frequently discover a max-margin solution (Soudry et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2019; Chizat & Bach, 2020; Morwani et al., 2023), we use the max-margin weights to describe a normative solution that the model implements to solve this task.

  3. 3.

    Under the max-margin solution, we establish the scaling relationships and generalization patterns observed in Figure 3.

B.1 Simplified model

We use a single-layer single-head Transformer model, summarized in Section 3. To facilitate our analysis, we simplify this model in the following ways.

We merge the key-query matrices into a single H×HH\times H matrix 𝐌≡K⊺​Q\mathbf{M}\equiv K^{\intercal}Q, and merge the value matrix 𝐕\mathbf{V} with the hidden weights 𝐖1\mathbf{W}_{1} into a single H×HH\times H matrix 𝐖≡𝐖𝟏​𝐕\mathbf{W}\equiv\mathbf{W_{1}}\mathbf{V}. For inputs 𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱L\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{L}, our reparameterized Transformer computes the LLth logit yLy_{L} as

yL≡f⁡(𝐱1,…,𝐱L)=∑i=1Hri​ϕ​(𝐰i⋅𝐯L)y_{L}\equiv f(\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{L})=\sum_{i=1}^{H}r_{i}\phi(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{L}) (2)

where

𝐰r=(r1r2rH)𝐖=(|||𝐰1𝐰2⋯𝐰H|||)⊺.\mathbf{w}_{r}=\begin{pmatrix}r_{1}\\ r_{2}\\ \vdots\\ r_{H}\end{pmatrix}\quad\mathbf{W}=\begin{pmatrix}\Big|&\Big|&&\Big|\\ \mathbf{w}_{1}&\mathbf{w}_{2}&\cdots&\mathbf{w}_{H}\\ \Big|&\Big|&&\Big|\\ \end{pmatrix}^{\intercal}\,.

and

𝐯L\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{L} =a1​L​𝐱1+…+aL​L​𝐱L\displaystyle=a_{1L}\,\mathbf{x}_{1}+\ldots+a_{LL}\,\mathbf{x}_{L}
ai​j\displaystyle a_{ij} =softmax​(1H​𝐱i⊺​𝐌𝐱j)\displaystyle=\text{softmax}\,\left(\frac{1}{H}\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\intercal}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}_{j}\right)

To simplify the analysis and unify the treatment of the direct prediction and reasoning trace cases, we ignore autoregressive generation in the RT model and consider classification accuracy only on the final logit, after a correct chain has been presented. Doing so constitutes an upper bound on the RT model’s performance. We nonetheless identify generalization weaknesses in the RT model independent of the autoregressive failures commonly posited as the source of failure for chain-of-thought prompting (Bengio et al., 2015; Schmidt, 2019; Wu et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025).

Sample-coordinate representation.

We next describe a sample-coordinate representation of the hidden weights 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i}. From Eq (2), it is evident that the gradient of yLy_{L} with respect to 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} is

∂yL∂𝐰i\displaystyle\frac{\partial y_{L}}{\partial\mathbf{w}_{i}} ∝𝐯L\displaystyle\propto\mathbf{v}_{L}
=a1​L​𝐱1+…+aL​L​𝐱L\displaystyle=a_{1L}\,\mathbf{x}_{1}+\ldots+a_{LL}\,\mathbf{x}_{L}

which is a sum over input embeddings 𝐱ℓ\mathbf{x}_{\ell}. Hence, if we train our model using gradient descent, all updates to 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} can be expressed as a linear combination of input embeddings. At the end of training, we may decompose 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} as

𝐰i=𝐰i0+c1i​𝐱1+c2i​𝐱2+…+cVi​𝐱V,\mathbf{w}_{i}=\mathbf{w}_{i}^{0}+c_{1}^{i}\mathbf{x}_{1}+c_{2}^{i}\mathbf{x}_{2}+\ldots+c_{V}^{i}\mathbf{x}_{V}\,,

If we assume the model begins with a zero or very small initialization, then 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} can be wholly characterized by the sample coordinates c1,c2,…​cVc_{1},c_{2},\ldots c_{V}, so called because they correspond to the coordinates of 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} in the span of the training samples. We study solutions to the TI task in this sample-coordinate space, ignoring the effect of the initialization. Indeed, we train our Transformers in a rich learning regime, where the influence of initialization is diminished. Sample coordinates are superficially similar to the dual coefficients that weight the contribution of training examples in kernel methods.

Note that

𝐰i⋅𝐱1=𝐰i0⋅𝐱1+c1i​‖𝐱1‖2+∑ℓ=2Vcℓi​(𝐱1⋅𝐱ℓ).\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{1}=\mathbf{w}_{i}^{0}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{1}+c_{1}^{i}||\mathbf{x}_{1}||^{2}+\sum_{\ell=2}^{V}c_{\ell}^{i}(\mathbf{x}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{\ell})\,. (3)

Since input embeddings are sampled from an isotropic standard Gaussian, we have that

𝔼⁡[‖𝐱1‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[||\mathbf{x}_{1}||^{2}] =Θ⁡(H)\displaystyle=\Theta\left(H\right)
