Hence, for very wide models H≫VH\gg V, we conclude that 1H​𝐰i⋅𝐱1≈c1i\frac{1}{H}\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{1}\approx c_{1}^{i} (we consider this condition more carefully below starting with Proposition B.2). We may therefore interpret our model as

yL≈H​∑i=1Hri​ϕ​(a1​L​c1i+…+aL​L​cLi).y_{L}\approx H\sum_{i=1}^{H}r_{i}\phi(a_{1L}\,c_{1}^{i}+\ldots+a_{LL}\,c_{L}^{i})\,.

When we analyze the margin of our model, we will frequently drop the extra factor of HH, which serves only to change the scale of the margin without impacting the classification. Later, when we report results based on estimated sample coordinates, we estimate the sample coordinate for 𝐱\mathbf{x} from a weight vector 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} precisely as c^i=1H​𝐰i⋅𝐱\hat{c}^{i}=\frac{1}{H}\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}.

Uniform attention weights.

Our final simplification is to assume that the attention weights are uniform: a1​L=a2​L=…=aL​L=1La_{1L}=a_{2L}=\ldots=a_{LL}=\frac{1}{L}. This rather drastic simplification is nonetheless supported by empirical measurements (Figure 4). We also give the following intuition for why the model settles on uniform attention on our TI task, based on max-margin considerations.

Let 𝒳={𝐱ℓ1,𝐱ℓ2,…,𝐱ℓL}\mathcal{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_{\ell_{1}},\mathbf{x}_{\ell_{2}},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{\ell_{L}}\} be the set of training examples with length LL, labeled by the function y⁡(𝐱ℓ1,…,𝐱ℓL)=±1y(\mathbf{x}_{\ell_{1}},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{\ell_{L}})=\pm 1. Then the margin is given by

δ=minℓ1,…,ℓL⁡y⁡(𝐱ℓ1,…,𝐱ℓL)​∑iri​ϕ​(aℓ1​ℓL​cℓ1i+…+aℓL​ℓL​cℓLi),\delta=\min_{\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{L}}\,y(\mathbf{x}_{\ell_{1}},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{\ell_{L}})\sum_{i}r_{i}\phi(a_{{\ell_{1}}\ell_{L}}\,c_{\ell_{1}}^{i}+\ldots+a_{{\ell_{L}}\ell_{L}}\,c_{\ell_{L}}^{i})\,,

subject to ∑iri2=1\sum_{i}r_{i}^{2}=1 and ∑i​j(cji)2=1\sum_{ij}\left(c_{j}^{i}\right)^{2}=1 (or equivalent norm constraints). Suppose there exists a unique training example that lies on the margin, given by indices m1,…,mLm_{1},\ldots,m_{L}. Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be the set of hidden activation indices ii such that am1​mL​cm1i+…+amL​mL​cmLi>0a_{{m_{1}}{m_{L}}}c_{m_{1}}^{i}+\ldots+a_{{m_{L}}{m_{L}}}c_{m_{L}}^{i}>0. Then the magnitude of the margin is given by

|δ|=am1​mL​∑i∈ℐri​cm1i+…+amL​mL​∑i∈ℐri​cmLi.|\delta|=a_{{m_{1}}{m_{L}}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}r_{i}c_{m_{1}}^{i}+\ldots+a_{{m_{L}}{m_{L}}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}r_{i}c_{m_{L}}^{i}\,.

If the model attains perfect training accuracy (as it does empirically), then δ=|δ|\delta=|\delta|. Attention weights must sum to 1, so they form a convex sum over elements ∑i∈ℐri​cmti≡et\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}r_{i}c_{m_{t}}^{i}\equiv e_{t}. Given free choice over the attention weights, to maximize the margin, we could allocate all weight to the index arg​maxt⁡et\argmax_{t}e_{t}. Similarly, given free choice over the magnitudes of elements ete_{t}, we could allocate all available weight (allowed under our norm constraints) to the index arg​maxt⁡amt,mL\argmax_{t}a_{m_{t},m_{L}}.

Suppose we set am1,mL=1a_{m_{1},m_{L}}=1 and increased the weight of e1=∑i∈ℐri​cm1ie_{1}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}r_{i}c_{m_{1}}^{i}. Then the margin on the training example indexed by m1,…,mLm_{1},\ldots,m_{L} is now large, but it may no longer lie on the margin. The new example that minimizes δ\delta may now be very small. Indeed, due to the symmetry of the transitive inference task, any symbol may appear in any position and any class with even probability across all training examples. Hence, if am1,mLa_{m_{1},m_{L}} and e1e_{1} are large, then there exists a training example m1,m2′,…,mL′m_{1},m_{2}^{\prime},\ldots,m_{L}^{\prime} in the opposite class as m1,…,mLm_{1},\ldots,m_{L}, with a very small or very negative margin because of our weight allocation.

Hence, because of this symmetry, we conjecture that the magnitude of each ete_{t} tends to remain about the same in the max margin set, and no position or symbol is favored above any other. The margin cannot be increased by concentrating attention on one position or symbol, only shrunk. Thus, uniform attention weights are favorable, and we confirm empirically in Figure 4 that a trained transformer indeed exhibits uniform attention weights on our task.

With uniform attention weights a1​L=…=aL​L=1La_{1L}=\ldots=a_{LL}=\frac{1}{L}, our model simplifies down to

yL=1L​∑i=1Hri​ϕ​(𝐰i⋅(𝐱1+⋯+𝐱L)).y_{L}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{H}r_{i}\phi(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot(\mathbf{x}_{1}+\cdots+\mathbf{x}_{L}))\,.

B.2 Max-margin solution

Neural networks trained on a classification objective routinely discover the max-margin solution (Soudry et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2019; Chizat & Bach, 2020). This observation has been productively applied to explaining the features in trained models (Morwani et al., 2023; Tong & Pehlevan, 2025). We study the structure of the max margin weights for our transitive inference task, and use it to form the basis of a normative solution our model should learn. We then use this solution to reveal how its properties constrain the scaling relationships between model width HH and task parameters B,DB,D.

Following Morwani et al. (2023), we consider the max average margin as a reasonable proxy to the strict max margin. If training examples are sampled from the distribution (𝐱1,…,𝐱L),y∼𝒟(\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{L}),y\sim\mathcal{D}, then the average margin is given by

δ¯=𝔼𝒟​[yL​∑i=1Hri​ϕ​(𝐰i⋅(𝐱1+…+𝐱L))].\overline{\delta}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\left[\frac{y}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{H}r_{i}\,\phi(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot(\mathbf{x}_{1}+\ldots+\mathbf{x}_{L}))\right]\,.

Denote the max margin solution to be

{ri∗,𝐰i∗}=\displaystyle\{r_{i}^{*},\mathbf{w}_{i}^{*}\}= arg​maxri,𝐰i⁡δ¯\displaystyle\argmax_{r_{i},\mathbf{w}_{i}}\,\overline{\delta}
subject​to​|ri|=‖𝐰i‖=1\displaystyle\text{subject}\,\text{to}\;|r_{i}|=||\mathbf{w}_{i}||=1

Note, we apply our norm constraint to individual activations |ri||r_{i}| and ‖𝐰i‖||\mathbf{w}_{i}||. This scheme is more restrictive than a global constraint where for instance ∑iri2=1\sum_{i}r_{i}^{2}=1 and ∑i‖𝐰i‖2=1\sum_{i}||\mathbf{w}_{i}||^{2}=1. Our choice of constraints reflects the assumption that each activation contributes equally to the final classification, and that the margin cannot be improved by weighting some activations heavier than others. We also find empirically that the sign of each rir_{i} tends to remain the same throughout training. We later show in Figure 5 that the structure of the max margin solution under these assumptions is descriptive of the actual weights learned by a model after training.

Suppose that training examples with positive label y=1y=1 have distribution 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+} and examples with negative label y=−1y=-1 have distribution 𝒟−\mathcal{D}^{-}. Denote sets of indices ℐ+={i:ri∗>0}\mathcal{I}^{+}=\{i:r_{i}^{*}>0\} and ℐ−={i:ri∗<0}\mathcal{I}^{-}=\{i:r_{i}^{*}<0\}. Denote the input embeddings by 𝐱¯=1L​(𝐱1+…+𝐱L)\overline{\mathbf{x}}=\frac{1}{L}(\mathbf{x}_{1}+\ldots+\mathbf{x}_{L}). Then by linearity of expectation,

δ¯\displaystyle\overline{\delta} =12​∑i∈ℐ+(𝔼𝒟+​[ϕ⁡(𝐰i⋅𝐱¯)]−𝔼𝒟−​[ϕ⁡(𝐰i⋅𝐱¯)])\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{+}}\left[\phi(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\overline{\mathbf{x}})\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{-}}\left[\phi(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\overline{\mathbf{x}})\right]\right)
−12∑j∈ℐ−(𝔼𝒟+[ϕ(𝐰j⋅𝐱¯)]−𝔼𝒟−[ϕ(𝐰j⋅𝐱¯)]).\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}^{-}}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{+}}\left[\phi(\mathbf{w}_{j}\cdot\overline{\mathbf{x}})\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{-}}\left[\phi(\mathbf{w}_{j}\cdot\overline{\mathbf{x}})\right]\right)\,. (4)

Under the sample-coordinate representation, we have that

LH​𝐰i⋅𝐱¯≈c1i+…+cLi\frac{L}{H}\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\overline{\mathbf{x}}\approx c_{1}^{i}+\ldots+c_{L}^{i}\,

so

LH​ϕ​(𝐰i⋅𝐱¯)≈(c1i+…+cLi)​𝟙c1i+…+cLi>0.\frac{L}{H}\phi(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\overline{\mathbf{x}})\approx(c_{1}^{i}+\ldots+c_{L}^{i})\mathbbm{1}_{c_{1}^{i}+\ldots+c_{L}^{i}>0}\,.

We characterize the structure of the max margin solution in our sample-coordinate space defined by ctic_{t}^{i}.

We begin with an intuitive discussion before presenting a formal result. We use a superscript on 𝐱tn\mathbf{x}_{t}^{n} to denote that symbol embedding 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} lies on branch nn (while the index tt would now correspond to a particular depth within branch nn). Given input embeddings 𝐱1m,𝐱2n,…,𝐱Ln\mathbf{x}_{1}^{m},\mathbf{x}_{2}^{n},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{L}^{n}, our scheme for constructing the reasoning trace requires that all symbols 𝐱2n,𝐱3n,…,𝐱Ln\mathbf{x}_{2}^{n},\mathbf{x}_{3}^{n},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{L}^{n} lie on the same branch. The symbol 𝐱1m\mathbf{x}_{1}^{m} shares the same branch m=nm=n only if the input has a positive label y=1y=1. Otherwise when y=−1y=-1, the symbol 𝐱1m\mathbf{x}_{1}^{m} lies on a different branch m≠nm\neq n. In cases where y=1y=1 (and all symbols lie on the same branch), our margin over these examples is

12​∑i∈ℐ+𝔼𝒟+​[ϕ⁡(𝐰i⋅𝐱¯)]−12​∑j∈ℐ−𝔼𝒟+​[ϕ⁡(𝐰j⋅𝐱¯)].\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{+}}[\phi(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\overline{\mathbf{x}})]-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}^{-}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{+}}[\phi(\mathbf{w}_{j}\cdot\overline{\mathbf{x}})]\,.

Hence for i∈ℐ+i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}, the margin is maximized when the sum c1i,n+…+cLi,nc_{1}^{i,n}+\ldots+c_{L}^{i,n} is large. However, for indices j∈ℐ−j\in\mathcal{I}^{-}, the margin is maximized when the sum c1j,m+…+cLj,nc_{1}^{j,m}+\ldots+c_{L}^{j,n} is very small or negative. In this way, we want the quantity c1i,n+…+cLi,nc_{1}^{i,n}+\ldots+c_{L}^{i,n} to be large when 𝐱1n\mathbf{x}_{1}^{n} is on the same branch nn as the remaining symbols 𝐱2n,…,𝐱Ln\mathbf{x}_{2}^{n},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{L}^{n}, suggesting that c1i,n>0c_{1}^{i,n}>0 when c2i,n,…,cLi,n>0c_{2}^{i,n},\ldots,c_{L}^{i,n}>0. However, when the first symbol belongs to a different branch m≠nm\neq n, we desire for c1i,m+…+cLi,nc_{1}^{i,m}+\ldots+c_{L}^{i,n} to be small or negative, suggesting that the sign of symbols cti,mc_{t}^{i,m} should be the opposite of the sign for symbols cti,nc_{t}^{i,n} lying on a different branch nn. We might therefore expect that activations for i∈ℐ+i\in\mathcal{I}^{+} may have a structure such that all sample coordinates sharing a branch should also share the same sign, some positive and some negative.

The opposite is true when considering the case y=−1y=-1:

−12∑i∈ℐ+𝔼𝒟−[ϕ(𝐰i)⋅𝐱¯]+12∑j∈ℐ−𝔼𝒟−[ϕ(𝐰j)⋅𝐱¯].-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{-}}[\phi(\mathbf{w}_{i})\cdot\overline{\mathbf{x}}]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}^{-}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{-}}[\phi(\mathbf{w}_{j})\cdot\overline{\mathbf{x}}]\,.

For activations corresponding to an index i∈ℐ+i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}, the margin is now maximized when the sum c1i,n+…+cLi,nc_{1}^{i,n}+\ldots+c_{L}^{i,n} is small or negative; for index j∈ℐ−j\in\mathcal{I}^{-}, the margin is maximized when the sum c1j,m+…+cLj,nc_{1}^{j,m}+\ldots+c_{L}^{j,n} is large. The first condition on c1j,n+…+cLj,nc_{1}^{j,n}+\ldots+c_{L}^{j,n} suggests that all coordinates sharing the same branch nn should be negative or balanced in sign, whereas the second condition on c1j,m+…+cLj,nc_{1}^{j,m}+\ldots+c_{L}^{j,n} suggests that at least some coordinates should be large and positive. Hence, we might expect that activations for j∈ℐ−j\in\mathcal{I}^{-} should exhibit a mixed proportion of positive and negative sample coordinates across branches.

We can formalize these intuitions in the case where L=2L=2 (corresponding to the direct prediction model) and the magnitude of |ctn||c_{t}^{n}| is the same across all symbols, in Proposition B.1 below. We find empirically that the structure of weights in trained models are consistent with this analysis (Figure 5).

Proposition B.1.

Under the sample-coordinate representation, suppose that the magnitude of sample coordinates |cki,n||c_{k}^{i,n}| is the same across all depth indices kk, activation indices ii, and branch indices nn. If L=2L=2 and the task parameters B,D≫1B,D\gg 1, then the following properties hold for the set of sample coordinates cki,nc_{k}^{i,n} that maximize the margin in Eq 4:

  • •

    For activation indices i∈ℐ+i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}, sign​(cki,n)=sign​(ck′i,n)\text{sign}(c_{k}^{i,n})=\text{sign}(c_{k^{\prime}}^{i,n}) for all k,k′∈[D]k,k^{\prime}\in[D]. In words, all coordinates that share the same branch also have the same sign. Furthermore, exactly half of the branches have coordinates with positive sign, and half of branches have coordinates with negative sign.

  • •

    For activation indices j∈ℐ−j\in\mathcal{I}^{-}, ∑k𝟙{ckj,n>0}=∑k𝟙{ckj,n′>0}\sum_{k}\mathbbm{1}\{{c_{k}^{j,n}>0}\}=\sum_{k}\mathbbm{1}\{c_{k}^{j,n^{\prime}}>0\} for all n,n′∈[B]n,n^{\prime}\in[B]. In words, the proportion of positive coordinates is the same across all branches.

Proof.

Given a training example that consists of the two input embeddings 𝐱km,𝐱ℓn\mathbf{x}_{k}^{m},\mathbf{x}_{\ell}^{n}, in sample coordinates we have

1Hϕ(𝐰i⋅(𝐱km+𝐱ℓn))=(cki,m+cℓi,n)𝟙{cki,m+cℓi,n>0}.\frac{1}{H}\phi(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot(\mathbf{x}_{k}^{m}+\mathbf{x}_{\ell}^{n}))=(c_{k}^{i,m}+c_{\ell}^{i,n})\mathbbm{1}\{c_{k}^{i,m}+c_{\ell}^{i,n}>0\}\,.

Since |cki,m|=|cℓi,n||c_{k}^{i,m}|=|c_{\ell}^{i,n}|, we can rewrite our indicator as 𝟙​{(cki,m>0)∩(cℓi,n>0)}\mathbbm{1}\{(c_{k}^{i,m}>0)\,\cap\,(c_{\ell}^{i,n}>0)\}, and

𝔼𝒟[ϕ(𝐰i⋅(𝐱km+𝐱ℓn))∝Pr(cki,m>0∩cℓi,n>0).\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\phi(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot(\mathbf{x}_{k}^{m}+\mathbf{x}_{\ell}^{n}))\propto\Pr(c_{k}^{i,m}>0\,\cap\,c_{\ell}^{i,n}>0)\,.

Define μi,m=Pr⁡(cki,m>0)\mu_{i,m}=\Pr(c_{k}^{i,m}>0) for an index kk sampled uniformly at random from branch mm. Recall that examples with positive label y=1y=1 are sampled from the same branch. Hence for large task depth DD, we have

Pr𝒟+⁡(cki,m>0∩cℓi,n>0)=1B​∑m=1Bμi,m2.\Pr\nolimits_{\mathcal{D^{+}}}(c_{k}^{i,m}>0\,\cap\,c_{\ell}^{i,n}>0)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{m=1}^{B}\mu_{i,m}^{2}\,.

Recall that examples with negative label y=−1y=-1 are sampled from different branches. Hence for large task breadth BB, we have

Pr𝒟−⁡(cki,m>0∩cℓi,n>0)=μ¯i2≡(1B​∑m=1Bμi,m)2.\Pr\nolimits_{\mathcal{D^{-}}}(c_{k}^{i,m}>0\,\cap\,c_{\ell}^{i,n}>0)=\overline{\mu}_{i}^{2}\equiv\left(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{m=1}^{B}\mu_{i,m}\right)^{2}\,.

Altogether then, we have

E𝒟+​[ϕ⁡(𝐰i⋅𝐱¯)]−𝔼𝒟−​[ϕ⁡(𝐰i⋅𝐱¯)]∝(1B​∑b=1Bμi,m2)−μ¯i2.E_{\mathcal{D}^{+}}\left[\phi(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\overline{\mathbf{x}})\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{-}}\left[\phi(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\overline{\mathbf{x}})\right]\propto\left(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mu_{i,m}^{2}\right)-\overline{\mu}_{i}^{2}\,. (5)

If i∈ℐ+i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}, maximizing the margin in Eq (4) requires maximizing Eq (5). Otherwise if i∈ℐ−i\in\mathcal{I}^{-}, then maximizing the margin requires minimizing Eq (5). We would therefore like to characterize the extrema of this expression.

We first characterize the maximum, revealing the structure of activations i∈ℐ+i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}. Note that μi,m∈[0,1]\mu_{i,m}\in[0,1], so we must have that μb2≤μb\mu_{b}^{2}\leq\mu_{b}, with equality when μi,m=1\mu_{i,m}=1 or μi,m=0\mu_{i,m}=0. This suggests that

(1B​∑m=1Bμi,b2)−μ¯i2≤μ¯i−μ¯i2,\left(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{m=1}^{B}\mu_{i,b}^{2}\right)-\overline{\mu}_{i}^{2}\leq\overline{\mu}_{i}-\overline{\mu}_{i}^{2}\,,

again with equality if all μi,m\mu_{i,m} equal either 00 or 11. The quantity μ¯i−μ¯i2\overline{\mu}_{i}-\overline{\mu}_{i}^{2} is maximized for μ¯i=12\overline{\mu}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}. In this way, the outcome that μi,m\mu_{i,m} be either 00 or 11 corresponds to the condition that all coordinates within a task branch share the same sign. The outcome that μ¯i=12\overline{\mu}_{i}=\frac{1}{2} corresponds to the condition that half the task branches consist of positive coordinates, and the other half consist of negative coordinates.

Now for the minimum (relating to activations i∈ℐ−i\in\mathcal{I}^{-}), we observe that Eq (5) is always non-negative. Indeed, if we interpret μi,m\mu_{i,m} as draws from a random variable, then Eq (5) is simply its variance. This expression is minimized when (1B​∑m=1Bμi,b2)=μ¯i2\left(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{m=1}^{B}\mu_{i,b}^{2}\right)=\overline{\mu}_{i}^{2}, which occurs when μi,b=μ¯i\mu_{i,b}=\overline{\mu}_{i}. This result corresponds to the condition that the proportion of positive coordinates is the same across all task branches. ∎

Proposition B.1 holds only under specific conditions, but as our discussion above illustrates, we expect the general structure of the max margin solution to continue holding for large LL and unconstrained coordinate magnitudes. Indeed, we find empirically that trained models tends to obey this max margin structure (Figure 5).

B.3 Scaling relationships

Armed with a general understanding of the max margin solution, we turn our attention to understanding the scaling relationships uncovered in Figure 3 and summarized in Table 1, which illustrates the scalings between task depth, breadth, and model width required to saturate the training accuracy on the transitive inference task.

Our approach for studying these scalings proceeds as follows. Given a hidden weight 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} and symbol embedding 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1}, Eq (3) suggests that 1H​𝐰i⋅𝐱1≈c1i\frac{1}{H}\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{1}\approx c_{1}^{i} (or for any other index j≠1j\neq 1, without loss of generality), provided that H≫VH\gg V. We formalize this intuition below in Proposition B.2.

Proposition B.2.

Let 𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱V\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{V} be iid draws from a standard Gaussian with dimension HH. Suppose c1,c2,…,cVc_{1},c_{2},\ldots,c_{V} are sample coordinates such that |c1|=|c2|=…=|cV|=c|c_{1}|=|c_{2}|=\ldots=|c_{V}|=c, for some fixed finite cc, and 𝐰=c1​𝐱1+c2​𝐱2+…+cV​𝐱V\mathbf{w}=c_{1}\mathbf{x}_{1}+c_{2}\mathbf{x}_{2}+\ldots+c_{V}\mathbf{x}_{V}. If V=o⁡(H)V=o(H), then as H→∞H\rightarrow\infty, 1H​𝐰⋅𝐱1\frac{1}{H}\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{1} converges in probability to c1c_{1}.

Proof.

We observe that

1H​𝐰⋅𝐱1=c1H​‖𝐱1‖2+1H​∑j=2Vcj​(𝐱1⋅𝐱j).\frac{1}{H}\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{1}=\frac{c_{1}}{H}||\mathbf{x}_{1}||^{2}+\frac{1}{H}\sum_{j=2}^{V}c_{j}(\mathbf{x}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{j})\,.

The Law of Large Numbers suggests that the quantity c1​‖𝐱1‖2/Hc_{1}||\mathbf{x}_{1}||^{2}/H converges almost surely to c1c_{1}.

Denote the sum over cross products as

SH=1H​∑j=2Vcj​(𝐱1⋅𝐱j)S_{H}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{j=2}^{V}c_{j}(\mathbf{x}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{j}) (6)

We observe that

𝔼⁡[SH]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[S_{H}\right] =0\displaystyle=0
Var(SH)\displaystyle\Var\left(S_{H}\right) <c2​VH\displaystyle<c^{2}\frac{V}{H}

Under Chebyshev’s inequality, for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, we must have that

Pr[|SH|>ε]≤c2​Vε2​H.\Pr\left[|S_{H}|>\varepsilon\right]\leq\frac{c^{2}V}{\varepsilon^{2}H}\,.

Since V=o⁡(H)V=o(H), the quantity |SH||S_{H}| must converge in probability to 0. In this way, we have overall that 1H​𝐰⋅𝐱1→c1\frac{1}{H}\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{1}\rightarrow c_{1} in probability. ∎

This proposition indicates that, so long as the number of symbols VV remains small with respect to the hidden dimension HH, we do indeed have that 1H​𝐰i⋅𝐱1=c1i\frac{1}{H}\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{1}=c_{1}^{i} as HH increases. Similar to our max margin argument formalized in Proposition B.1, we require that the magnitude of all coordinates cc are the same. As before, the symmetry of the transitive inference task suggests that we generally expect the magnitudes of these coordinates to be similar, though we explore a notable exception below in Section B.3.2. We next apply Proposition B.2 to understand scaling relationships in our transitive inference task.

B.3.1 Depth-wise scaling

Our TI task is parameterized by two numbers: breadth BB (the number of chains of syllogisms) and depth DD (the length of each chain). The total number of unique symbols VV, ignoring special tokens for padding and termination, must therefore be V=B​DV=BD.

Direct prediction model.

To explain the scaling relationships in Figure 3, we first fix BB while increasing DD and HH to understand depth-wise scaling with model width. Recall from Section B.2: the max margin solution requires that, for weights 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} corresponding to a positive activation index i∈ℐ+i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}, coordinates for symbols that share the same branch must also share the same sign. That is, for symbol embeddings 𝐱kn,𝐱ℓn\mathbf{x}_{k}^{n},\mathbf{x}_{\ell}^{n}, we require that sign​(𝐰i⋅𝐱kn)=sign​(𝐰i⋅𝐱ℓn)\text{sign}(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{k}^{n})=\text{sign}(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{\ell}^{n}). However, since V=Θ⁡(D)V=\Theta(D), if D=ω⁡(H)D=\omega(H), then V=ω⁡(H)V=\omega(H). Proposition B.2 no longer holds, and we cannot guarantee that sign​(𝐰i⋅𝐱kn)=sign​(𝐰i⋅𝐱ℓn)\text{sign}(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{k}^{n})=\text{sign}(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{\ell}^{n}). Indeed, if the magnitudes of all sample coordinates remain approximately the same, then our sum over cross terms in Eq (6) explodes, leaving us with chance-level output: Pr⁡(sign​(𝐰i⋅𝐱kn)=sign​(𝐰i⋅𝐱ℓn))=1/2\Pr(\text{sign}(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{k}^{n})=\text{sign}(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{\ell}^{n}))=1/2. For this reason, D=𝒪⁡(H)D=\mathcal{O}(H) poses a natural upper bound on scaling DD, agreeing with the linear scaling we observe empirically for direct prediction models in Figure 3.

In general, we expect this requirement for sign-sharing among weights with positive activation indices to be the bottleneck that determines the scaling. For weights with negative activation index, our max-margin solution only expects that in each branch, a portion of sample coordinates are positive, and a portion are negative. This mild condition is satisfied at initialization, and we conjecture that its impact on scaling is minimal.

RT model.

Given this argument for linear scaling, why does the RT model settle on a markedly slower depth-wise scaling? The reason may be that the model’s context length also grows with DD. To construct a chain for a task with depth DD, the RT model requires L=Θ⁡(D)L=\Theta(D) context tokens 𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱L\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{L}, of which 𝐱2,…,𝐱L\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{L} enumerate over all symbols belonging to a branch. Hence, an increasing segment of the context is dedicated to this enumeration, potentially diluting the desired signal: whether 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1} belongs in the same branch as the others.

We may analyze this setup as a distinguishability problem. Recall that symbol embeddings are sampled from a standard Gaussian 𝐱∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈H)\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{H}) and fixed throughout training. If HH is the embedding dimension, then with respect to the randomness of the embeddings, the distribution of a negative example FF may be 1L​(𝐱1+𝐱2+…​𝐱L)∼F≡𝒩⁡(𝟎,1L​𝐈)\frac{1}{L}(\mathbf{x}_{1}+\mathbf{x}_{2}+\ldots\mathbf{x}_{L})\sim F\equiv\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\frac{1}{L}\mathbf{I}\right). For a positive example, 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1} is duplicated at some point in the enumeration 𝐱2,…,𝐱L\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{L}, so the distribution of a positive example 𝐓\mathbf{T} becomes 1L​(2​𝐱1+𝐱2+…​𝐱L−1)∼T≡𝒩⁡(𝟎,2+LL2​𝐈H)\frac{1}{L}(2\mathbf{x}_{1}+\mathbf{x}_{2}+\ldots\mathbf{x}_{L-1})\sim T\equiv\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\frac{2+L}{L^{2}}\mathbf{I}_{H}\right). The model’s ability to learn the task becomes a problem of statistical indistinguishability: given a sample from either FF or TT, with what probability can the model determine its origin? We answer this question with help from Proposition B.3, which establishes an upper bound on the total variation distance (TV) between FF and TT.

This description is precise only if we resample the embeddings between each draw of a positive or negative example. It may, however, continue to be accurate when the vocabulary size is large, and inputs are not frequently repeated. We indeed observe that this framing is predictive for the empirically observed scaling.

Proposition B.3.

Define the distributions F≡𝒩⁡(𝟎,1L​𝐈H)F\equiv\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\frac{1}{L}\mathbf{I}_{H}) and T≡𝒩⁡(𝟎,2+LL2​𝐈H)T\equiv\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\frac{2+L}{L^{2}}\mathbf{I}_{H}). Let TV​(F,T)\text{TV}(F,T) be the total variation distance between FF and TT. Then for L→∞L\rightarrow\infty, TV​(F,T)=𝒪​(H/L)\text{TV}(F,T)=\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{H}/L).

Proof.

From Pinsker’s inequality, we know that

TV​(F,T)≤12DK​L(F||T).\text{TV}(F,T)\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}D_{KL}(F\,||\,T)}\,. (7)

From the definitions of FF and TT,

DK​L(F||T)=H2(L2+L+log2+LL−1).D_{KL}(F\,||\,T)=\frac{H}{2}\left(\frac{L}{2+L}+\log\frac{2+L}{L}-1\right)\,.

Taylor expanding this quantity around L→∞L\rightarrow\infty reveals that

DK​L(F||T)\displaystyle D_{KL}(F\,||\,T) =H2​(2L2−163​L3+𝒪​(1L4))\displaystyle=\frac{H}{2}\left(\frac{2}{L^{2}}-\frac{16}{3L^{3}}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{L^{4}}\right)\right)
=𝒪⁡(HL2).\displaystyle=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{H}{L^{2}}\right)\,.

In this way, we see that the KL divergence is bounded asymptotically by 𝒪⁡(H/L2)\mathcal{O}(H/L^{2}). In fact, the function HL2\frac{H}{L^{2}} upper bounds the KL divergence for all LL. To see how, define u=2/Lu=2/L so that

g(u)≡2HDK​L(F||T)=11+u+log(1+u)−1.g(u)\equiv\frac{2}{H}D_{KL}(F\,||\,T)=\frac{1}{1+u}+\log(1+u)-1\,.

Let

f⁡(u)=u22−g⁡(u).f(u)=\frac{u^{2}}{2}-g(u)\,.

Then f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 and

f′​(u)=u2​(u+2)(1+u)2,\displaystyle f^{\prime}(u)=\frac{u^{2}(u+2)}{(1+u)^{2}},

so f′​(u)>0f^{\prime}(u)>0 for u>0u>0. Hence, we must have u22≥g⁡(u)\frac{u^{2}}{2}\geq g(u) for all u>0u>0. Substituting u=2/Lu=2/L, we must have that DK​L(F||T)≤H/L2D_{KL}(F\,||\,T)\leq H/L^{2} for all LL.

Substituting our upper bound for the KL divergence into Eq (7), we conclude that

TV​(F,T)=𝒪​(H/L).\text{TV}(F,T)=\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{H}/L)\,.

∎

Returning to our original question, our model is presented with a sample from either FF or TT, and must determine its origin. A classic result in statistical theory asserts that the probability of success is given by 12​(1+TV​(F,T))\frac{1}{2}(1+\text{TV}(F,T)) (see for instance Theorem 2.2 in Tsybakov (2009)). Since L=Θ⁡(D)L=\Theta(D), we expect that the model’s accuracy is also bounded by 12+𝒪⁡(H/D)\frac{1}{2}+\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{H}/D). The high-accuracy contour should therefore exhibit the scaling D=𝒪⁡(H)D=\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{H}), which agrees with the square-root scaling we observe in Figure 3.

B.3.2 Breadth-wise scaling

A direct application of our argument in Section B.3.1 suggests that breadth-wise scaling should also be linear. However, linear scaling may be exceeded if we also consider the possibility that the magnitude of sample coordinates differ between symbols.

Suppose we fix the task depth DD, and scale the task breadth BB with model width HH. Since the size of the vocabulary is V=B​DV=BD, as we increase BB, we note that V=Θ⁡(B)V=\Theta(B). As before, our max margin solution suggests that for a positive activation with index i∈ℐ+i\in\mathcal{I}^{+} and any two symbol embeddings 𝐱kn,𝐱ℓn\mathbf{x}_{k}^{n},\mathbf{x}_{\ell}^{n} which belong to the same branch nn, we require sign​(𝐰i⋅𝐱kn)=sign​(𝐰i⋅𝐱ℓn)\text{sign}(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{k}^{n})=\text{sign}(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{\ell}^{n}). If the magnitude of all sample coordinates cc is about the same, then Proposition B.2 suggests we should expect the scaling to be B=o⁡(H)B=o(H).

However, when scaling breadth, perhaps the structure of the task would allow us to bypass the assumption that all sample coordinates have the same magnitude. In particular, suppose that some fraction of the sample coordinates are zero. Their contribution to the cross sum in Eq (6) would be removed, and the vocabulary may be increased.

Our max margin construction in Section B.2 requires that all coordinates sharing a branch are uniformly positive or negative. What if we additionally allow some of them to be relatively small or zero? Since there are HH activations in our model, and BB total branches, suppose we allowed each activation to prioritize B/HB/H branches, and maintain nonzero coordinates only for these B/HB/H choices. Then Proposition B.2 would suggest that if we now scale as B/H=o⁡(H)B/H=o(H) (or equivalently, B=o⁡(H2)B=o(H^{2})), then we continue to have 1H​𝐰i⋅𝐱1=c1\frac{1}{H}\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{1}=c_{1}, and sign​(𝐰i⋅𝐱kn)=sign​(𝐰i⋅𝐱ℓn)\text{sign}(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{k}^{n})=\text{sign}(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{\ell}^{n}). This is consistent with our observed quadratic scaling in both DP and RT models.

If our models indeed distribute sample coordinates in this fashion, then we should observe a linear relationship between the number of large, positive sample coordinates and the task breadth. We empirically observe precisely this trend in Figure 6.

Distributing depth?

By distributing branches across HH activations, we attain a faster scaling than the linear rate suggested by our argument in Section B.3.1. Could the same strategy be employed to improve our rate when scaling by depth?

The answer turns out to be no, since doing so blocks us from classifying positive examples correctly. Suppose we distribute DD depths among HH activations, with each activation implementing nonzero coordinates for D/HD/H depths. Then the proportion of nonzero coordinates per activation is D/HD=1H\frac{D/H}{D}=\frac{1}{H}, which approaches zero as HH increases. Hence, there no longer exists a branch for which the proportion of positive coordinates is close to 1, which our max margin solution in Proposition B.1 requires to classify a positive example. For this reason, depth scaling remains limited to D=o⁡(H)D=o(H).

B.4 Generalization outcomes

We next turn our attention to length generalization, and study why length generalization deteriorates quickly direct-prediction models, but remains intact their reasoning trace counterparts.

B.4.1 DP model

We observe in Figure 3 that length generalization decays in our DP model as task breadth BB increases. In the following section, we consider why length generalization deteriorates, and ballpark estimate the rate at which it decays with BB.

We begin by providing a broad intuition for why test performance decays at all. Suppose we restrict our training distribution to relations with distance ≤k\leq k, then test on distances >k>k. Let 𝐰j\mathbf{w}_{j} be a weight vector with negative activation index j∈ℐ−j\in\mathcal{I}^{-}, and sample coordinates indexed by branch nn and depth kk, ckj,nc_{k}^{j,n}. Our max margin solution (Section B.2) suggests that a proportion of coordinates within a branch will be positive.

However, if k≪Dk\ll D, then the placement of these positive coordinates need not be uniform. Indeed, we should expect that cpj,n+cqj,nc_{p}^{j,n}+c_{q}^{j,n} is small or negative for d⁡(xpn,xqn)≤kd(x_{p}^{n},x_{q}^{n})\leq k, increasing the margin on these points in the training set. On the other hand, cpj,n+crj,nc_{p}^{j,n}+c_{r}^{j,n} has no such constraints when d⁡(xp,xr)>kd(x_{p},x_{r})>k, and may be correspondingly large. Indeed, some proportion of coordinates in each branch must be large and positive in order to produce correct negative classifications. Hence, positive coordinates will tend to have small or negative neighbors within kk distance. When longer distances are prompted at test time, these large, positive coordinates may be selected, increasing the contribution from negative activations. Activations with positive index are uniformly positive or negative within a branch, so the contribution from positive activations should remain the same for larger test distances as they are for shorter distances. The overall result is a false negative. Indeed, we find empirically that the vast majority of test error are false negatives (Figure 7).

B.5 Estimating the error.

Using these observations, we offer a back-of-the-envelope estimate for how test accuracy falls with increasing task breadth. We first conjecture how increasing breadth causes output logits to decrease, then use the rate of decrease to ballpark the classification accuracy, finding that test accuracy diminishes as 𝒪⁡(B−2)\mathcal{O}(B^{-2}).

For a direct prediction model, the gradient of the logit y^=∑i=1Hri​ϕ​(𝐰i⋅(𝐱pm+𝐱qn))\hat{y}=\sum_{i=1}^{H}r_{i}\,\phi(\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot(\mathbf{x}_{p}^{m}+\mathbf{x}_{q}^{n})) with respect to the hidden weights 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} is

∂y∂𝐰i∝𝐱pm+𝐱qn.\frac{\partial y}{\partial\mathbf{w}_{i}}\propto\mathbf{x}_{p}^{m}+\mathbf{x}_{q}^{n}\,.

This quantity is nonzero only if 𝐰i⋅(𝐱pm+𝐱qn)>0\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot(\mathbf{x}_{p}^{m}+\mathbf{x}_{q}^{n})>0, or equivalently in sample coordinates, cpi,m+cqi,n>0c_{p}^{i,m}+c_{q}^{i,n}>0. Consider also the contribution from the loss ℒ⁡(y,y^)\mathcal{L}(y,\hat{y}), for logit y^\hat{y} and label yy. If ℒ\mathcal{L} is binary cross entropy, then −sign​(∂ℒ∂𝓎^)=sign​(y)-\text{sign}\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathcal{\hat{y}}}\right)=\text{sign}(y). A gradient descent step in 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} on symbol embeddings 𝐱pm,𝐱qn\mathbf{x}_{p}^{m},\mathbf{x}_{q}^{n} therefore takes the following form, omitting the learning rate:

Δ𝐰i=sign(y)ri(𝐱pm+𝐱qn)𝟙{cpi,m+cqi,n>0}.\Delta\mathbf{w}_{i}=\text{sign}(y)\,r_{i}(\mathbf{x}_{p}^{m}+\mathbf{x}_{q}^{n})\mathbbm{1}\{c_{p}^{i,m}+c_{q}^{i,n}>0\}\,.

If cpi,m+cqi,n>0c_{p}^{i,m}+c_{q}^{i,n}>0, then the resulting change in the output logit for 𝐱pm,𝐱qn\mathbf{x}_{p}^{m},\mathbf{x}_{q}^{n} is simply

Δ​y^=ri​(Δ​𝐰i⋅(𝐱pm+𝐱qn))=sign​(y)​ri2​‖𝐱pm+𝐱qn‖2.\Delta\hat{y}=r_{i}(\Delta\mathbf{w}_{i}\cdot(\mathbf{x}_{p}^{m}+\mathbf{x}_{q}^{n}))=\text{sign}(y)\,r_{i}^{2}\,||\mathbf{x}_{p}^{m}+\mathbf{x}_{q}^{n}||^{2}\,.

Since ri2r_{i}^{2} and ‖𝐱pm+𝐱qn‖2||\mathbf{x}_{p}^{m}+\mathbf{x}_{q}^{n}||^{2} are positive, we see that sign​(Δ​y^)=sign​(y)\text{sign}(\Delta\hat{y})=\text{sign}(y). Intuitively, output logits increase for positive examples (y=1y=1) and decrease for negative examples (y=−1y=-1).

If an example is negative, then the component symbols must belong to different branches. For a symbol 𝐱pm\mathbf{x}_{p}^{m}, there are B−1B-1 other branches n≠mn\neq m from which to form a valid negative example. If a consistent proportion of these 𝒪⁡(B)\mathcal{O}(B) other pairings produce a negative contribution on the output logit, then we conjecture that the negative contribution to a logit over the course of training may also be of order 𝒪⁡(B)\mathcal{O}(B). Specifically, we assume that a logit decomposes as y^=y^0−β\hat{y}=\hat{y}_{0}-\beta, where y^=y^0\hat{y}=\hat{y}_{0} when B=2B=2 (the smallest possible task breadth BB) and β=𝒪⁡(B)\beta=\mathcal{O}(B).

In this way, as BB increases, all logits decrease, resulting in the false negative classifications we observe in Figure 7. To estimate the impact on classification accuracy, we need to estimate Pr⁡(y^>0)\Pr(\hat{y}>0). If the distribution of y^\hat{y} over test examples has a fixed variance σ2\sigma^{2}, then Cantelli’s inequality suggests that

Pr⁡(y^>0)=Pr⁡(y^−(y^0−β)>−(y^0−β))≤σ2σ2+(y^0−β)2.\Pr(\hat{y}>0)=\Pr(\hat{y}-(\hat{y}_{0}-\beta)>-(\hat{y}_{0}-\beta))\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\sigma^{2}+(\hat{y}_{0}-\beta)^{2}}\,.

If σ2\sigma^{2} does not vary with task breadth and β2≫σ2+y^02\beta^{2}\gg\sigma^{2}+\hat{y}_{0}^{2}, then Pr⁡(y^>0)=𝒪⁡(B−2)\Pr(\hat{y}>0)=\mathcal{O}\left(B^{-2}\right). In Figure 7, we confirm that this scaling is indeed accurate.

B.5.1 RT model

In Figure 3, we observe that generalization in RT models remains strong regardless of task breadth BB. This outcome is due to an inductive bias for a generalizing solution on our TI task facilitated by the reasoning trace. Specifically, we argue that for any test example, there exists a permutation that transforms it into a training example. In the absence of positional encodings, the model is invariant with respect to permutations in input position (up to the query token); if the model attains perfect training accuracy, then it attains perfect test accuracy also.

Proposition B.4.

Consider a task with training distance k≥2k\geq 2. Denote a test example as any sequence of symbols x1,x2,…,xLx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{L} such that d⁡(x1,x2)>kd(x_{1},x_{2})>k and x3,…,xLx_{3},\ldots,x_{L} enumerate the remaining symbols that belong in the same branch as x2x_{2}. Denote a training example similarly, except d⁡(x1,x2)≤kd(x_{1},x_{2})\leq k. Let π:ℕL−1→ℕL−1\pi:\mathbb{N}^{L-1}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}^{L-1} denote a permutation over L−1L-1 indices. Then for any test example, we may construct a permutation π\pi such that xπ⁡(1),xπ⁡(2),…,xLx_{\pi(1)},x_{\pi(2)},\ldots,x_{L} is a training example. Note, the query token xLx_{L} is not permuted.

Proof.

Given a test example x1,x2,…,xLx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{L}, the set of symbols x2,…,xLx_{2},\ldots,x_{L} enumerate all nodes in a branch. Then there must exist an index 2<j<L2<j<L such that d⁡(x1,xj)≤kd(x_{1},x_{j})\leq k. Because the test distance must be at least 2, there are at least 2 symbols that satisfy d⁡(x1,xj)≤kd(x_{1},x_{j})\leq k, allowing us to proceed even if d⁡(x1,xL)≤kd(x_{1},x_{L})\leq k. Construct a permutation by swapping x2x_{2} with xjx_{j}: π⁡(2)=j\pi(2)=j and π⁡(j)=2\pi(j)=2, while preserving the remaining indices. The set xπ⁡(2),…,xπ⁡(L−1)x_{\pi(2)},\ldots,x_{\pi(L-1)} continues to enumerate all nodes in a shared branch, while d⁡(xπ⁡(1),xπ⁡(2))<kd(x_{\pi(1)},x_{\pi(2)})<k. Thus, xπ⁡(1),xπ⁡(2),…,xLx_{\pi(1)},x_{\pi(2)},\ldots,x_{L} must be a training example. ∎

Proposition B.4 demonstrates that there always exists a permutation that transformers a test example into a train example. Our RT model is trained without positional encodings, and is therefore permutation invariant in positions up to the query token. If the model attains perfect training accuracy, then it should attain perfect test accuracy also, irrespective of task topology. Hence, we conclude that the RT model generalizes well on our TI task.

Appendix C Task and model details

Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/wtong98/boule-or-baguette. Exact configurations used to reproduce all plots can be found there.

The PITA dataset is available on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/datasets/williamtong105/pita.

Below, we summarize the details of our task setups and model configurations.

C.1 Making a PITA

The PITA dataset consists of statements in propositional logic together with a proof that demonstrates whether the statement is true or false. To convert these inputs into tokens that an LLM can process, we proceed through the following three steps:

  1. 1.

    Construct a proof

  2. 2.

    Translate the proof into Lean tactics and states

  3. 3.

    Structure the Lean output with XML delimiters

Appendix A provides a brief primer on propositional logic, and the process by which proofs may be constructed for propositional statements. Our proofs are constructed using a standard focused proof search procedure (Liang & Miller, 2009) based on the implementation from An et al. (2024). We then translate the resulting sequence of inference rules discovered by the search procedure into their corresponding Lean tactics, and poll the Lean proof assistant for intermediate proof states following each tactic application.

Following An et al. (2024), we also include backtrack tactics. These are a non-standard extension that directs Lean to resume tracking from the last unresolved proof state. Including backtrack allows us to “undo” erroneous proof steps. If the current sequence of tactics does not terminate in a tautology, backtrack brings us to the last state where we can apply a different tactic to explore a different branch of the proof. Figure 1 illustrates an example with a backtrack application. An et al. (2024) find that including these “mistake” demonstrations increases the model’s theorem-proving success by a substantial margin. Including backtrack also allows us to treat proofs for both true and false statements in a uniform way: if the model explores all reasonable tactics through backtrack and discovers no valid tautologies, then the proof must be false.

The backtrack tactic itself is implemented using the same procedure as in An et al. (2024). The proof search procedure constructs a tree of possible inference rule applications and their resulting proof states. A proof of a true statement is typically extracted as the shortest path between the starting state and a successful terminating leaf. A proof that includes backtrack may instead be constructed through a depth-first-search over this tree. Once the traversal encounters a failing terminal leaf, we inject a backtrack tactic to represent a return back to the last node with alternative paths, and proceed down the next viable branch.

Finally, given the sequence of tactics and states, we prepare the final input to the LLM by wrapping the tactics and state components in XML tags. The XML has the following structure:

<state id="0">
  <if> ... </if>       <!-- propositions that are given -->
  <if> ... </if>
  <then> ... </then>   <!-- goal proposition to demonstrate -->
</state>
<tactic> ... </tactic>
<state id="1"> ... </state>
<tactic> ... </tactic>
<state id="2"> ... </state>

<!-- ... and so on ...  -->

<backtrack to="m" />  <!-- possible backtrack to state ‘m‘ -->

<!-- ... and so on ...  -->

<state id="n">
   <complete />        <!-- indicates that the current subgoal is complete -->
</state>
<success />            <!-- or ‘<failure />‘ -->

If the propositional statement is true, we terminate in a <success /> tag. Otherwise, we terminate in a <failure /> tag. These tags constitute the special classification token that the model must output to indicate whether the statement is true or false. The entire sequence is then passed to the model-specific tokenizer and processed.

Models are trained on a prompt/completion input format, where loss is computed only on the completion tokens. The prompt is delineated by all tokens up to <state id="0">...</state>. The completion is the remainder of the proof for the RT model, or only the success/failure tag for the DP model. To ensure that the model tokenizer cleanly separates the prompt from the completion, we include an addition double bar || separating the prompt from completion, so the input looks like <state id="0">...</state>||<tactic>....

C.2 PITA split construction

PITA is composed of four different splits.

We discuss the details of each split and provide examples below.

Full.

This split corresponds to the full space of propositional statements, enumerating over all 3 connectives →,∨,∧\rightarrow,\vee,\wedge as well as propositional atoms ⊤,⊥\top,\bot and 3 variables p,q,rp,q,r. We exhaustively enumerate all statements up to 5 atoms in size (including enumerations over parenthetical groups), resulting in 3.6 million statements and 1.4 billion tokens. All examples are well under the 32K max context length of our models. Examples from this split are

p→p∨q\displaystyle p\rightarrow p\vee q
(\displaystyle( p∧q)→p∨(r→⊥)\displaystyle p\wedge q)\rightarrow p\vee(r\rightarrow\bot)
(\displaystyle( OPENp∨q)∧r∧⊤\displaystyle p\vee q)\wedge r\wedge\top
Imply.

This split corresponds to the implicational fragment of propositional logic. The setting is the same as Full, except we restrict to a single connective →\rightarrow. Somewhat surprisingly, doing so does not reduce the space of expressible propositions. The implicational fragment is functionally complete, so every propositional statement (interpreted as an input/output mapping between truth values) expressible in Full is also expressible in Imply. In this sense, the task is essentially the same as Full, but formatted differently. We exhaustively enumerate all statements up to 7 atoms in size, resulting in 11 million statements and 11.6 billion tokens. Virtually all examples are under the 32K max context length of our models. Examples from this split are

p→q→p\displaystyle p\rightarrow q\rightarrow p
(\displaystyle( p→⊥)→(p→⊤)\displaystyle p\rightarrow\bot)\rightarrow(p\rightarrow\top)
p→((q→r)→q)\displaystyle p\rightarrow((q\rightarrow r)\rightarrow q)
Or.

This split corresponds to a membership checking task expressed in propositional form. Each statement has the form p→q1∨q2∨…∨qnp\rightarrow q_{1}\vee q_{2}\vee\ldots\vee q_{n}, where exactly half of the statements have p∈{q1​…​qn}p\in\{q_{1}\ldots q_{n}\} (corresponding to true statements) and half the statements do not (corresponding to false statements). A random parenthetical grouping is sampled for the variables on the right hand side. The variable names for q1​…​qnq_{1}\ldots q_{n} are forced to be unique, and drawn from a pool of 100 thousand possible names to minimize the chance of name collisions. We sample 8.7 million of these statements, resulting in 78.5 billion tokens. A little less than 1 percent of these examples exceed the 32K max context length of our model; these examples are removed from the dataset. Examples from this split are

p→q1∨p∨q2∨q3∨q4\displaystyle p\rightarrow q_{1}\vee p\vee q_{2}\vee q_{3}\vee q_{4}
p→q1∨q2∨q3∨q4\displaystyle p\rightarrow q_{1}\vee q_{2}\vee q_{3}\vee q_{4}
p→q1∨q2∨q3∨q4∨p∨q5\displaystyle p\rightarrow q_{1}\vee q_{2}\vee q_{3}\vee q_{4}\vee p\vee q_{5}
PHP.

The pigeonhole principle is a classic counting argument that states the following: given mm pigeons and nn holes, if m>nm>n, there there must be at least one hole occupied by two or more pigeons. This statement can be framed in propositional logic in the following way. Let pi​jp_{ij} be the proposition “pigeon ii occupies hole jj”. Then the pigeonhole principle can be written as

⋀i=1m(pi​1∨pi​2​…∨pi​n)→⋁j=1n⋁i1≠i1(pi1​j∧pi2​j).\bigwedge_{i=1}^{m}\left(p_{i1}\vee p_{i2}\ldots\vee p_{in}\right)\rightarrow\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}\,\bigvee_{i_{1}\neq i_{1}}(p_{i_{1}j}\wedge p_{i_{2}j})\,. (8)

The antecedent corresponds to the condition that every pigeon must occupy a hole, and the consequent corresponds to the condition that at least one hole contains at least two pigeons. Proving these propositions reduces essentially to a constraint-satisfaction problem. Many such problems feature exponential time complexity to solve. Similarly, proving PHP propositions may take exponentially many steps in mm and nn, making them a common choice for stress-testing proof systems (Haken, 1985; Balsiger et al., 2000). We use a slightly harder version of this task (still commonly used a stress-test) where each pigeon may occupy only a subset of holes, and only a subset of pairs are checked for double-occupancy. We sample 36 of these conditions, and exhaustively enumerate over all possible parenthetical groupings, resulting in 51 thousand statements and 1.0 billion tokens. Examples from this split are

(\displaystyle( OPENp11∨p13)∧(p23)→(p12∧p22)∨(p13∧p23)\displaystyle p_{11}\vee p_{13})\wedge(p_{23})\rightarrow(p_{12}\wedge p_{22})\vee(p_{13}\wedge p_{23})
(\displaystyle( OPENp12)∧(p31∨p32∨p33)→(p11∧p21)\displaystyle p_{12})\wedge(p_{31}\vee p_{32}\vee p_{33})\rightarrow(p_{11}\wedge p_{21})
(\displaystyle( OPENp21∨p22)→(p11∧p21)∨(p11∧p31)∨(p22∧p32)\displaystyle p_{21}\vee p_{22})\rightarrow(p_{11}\wedge p_{21})\vee(p_{11}\wedge p_{31})\vee(p_{22}\wedge p_{32})

Each split is characterized by its depth and breadth. Depth is calculated as the unique number of proof states required to prove the statement, taken as the largest id number on the <state> tags. Hence, if the model backtracks to an earlier state, it is not double-counted.

Breadth is counted as the number of unique statements that can be enumerated for propositions of a given size, where size is measured by the number of atoms in the proposition. The or (∨\vee) and and (∧\wedge) connectives are commutative and associative, so we consider statements like (p∨q)∨r(p\vee q)\vee r to be the same as q∨(p∨r)q\vee(p\vee r), and do not count them as two unique statements. Furthermore, we distinguish propositional variables only by identity, rather than name. Hence, the statement p→q→pp\rightarrow q\rightarrow p is considered the same as p′→q′→p′p^{\prime}\rightarrow q^{\prime}\rightarrow p^{\prime}, though the variable names are different.

C.3 PITA model configurations

All models are finetuned using Hugging Face (Wolf et al., 2019). Inference is performed using vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). Specific training and inference setup are available on GitHub: https://github.com/wtong98/boule-or-baguette

Models are finetuned using QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) with rank r=16r=16, scaling factor α=32\alpha=32, and dropout probability p=0.05p=0.05. We target all linear modules. Our optimizer is 8 bit paged AdamW (Dettmers et al., 2021; Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017). We find that a relatively large learning rate of 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} works well, with a linear warm-up for 500 iterations followed by constant learning rate. We use a batch size of 32 examples. We find that accuracy typically plateaus after 2500 iterations (80 thousand examples) across all splits and prolonged training does not improve it, so we terminate training after 2500 iterations and evaluate the model. A maximum context length of 32 thousand tokens is enforced across all models. All models we evaluate have a native context window of at least 32 thousand.

Evaluation is conducted by allowing the model to autoregressively generate the next token until it produces a <success /> or <failure /> tag. If the model does not generate one of these tags before reaching its max context length, we terminate generation and designate that trial as a failure. Otherwise, classification accuracy is evaluated based on the terminating tag. Next tokens are sampled greedily.

C.4 TI task details

Our transitive inference task is similar to the forward-chaining setups prevalent in the TI literature (Lippl et al., 2024; Kay et al., 2024; Geerts et al., 2025). The key difference is that rather than use a single chain, we employ BB parallel chains of inferences, and the model must additionally learn cross-chain inferences.

We offer additional details on the sampling procedure for positive and negative examples. Suppose we have symbols sins_{i}^{n} indexed by depth ii and branch nn. To construct an example with label y=1y=1, we first sample a symbol sins_{i}^{n} uniformly at random, then sample its partner sjns_{j}^{n} where |j−i|≤k|j-i|\leq k during training and |j−i|>k|j-i|>k during testing, also uniformly at random from all possible choices. To construct an example with a negative label, we perform the same procedure but ensure that the two symbols fall on different branches, resulting in a pair sin,sjms_{i}^{n},s_{j}^{m} where n≠mn\neq m. Note, another valid way to construct a negative example would be to reverse a relation (e.g. s2n→s1ns_{2}^{n}\rightarrow s_{1}^{n}). We omit this case for simplicity, finding it unnecessary to reproduce the generalization characteristics we observed in PITA, and leave its exploration for future work.

C.5 TI model configurations

We use single-layer, single-head, decoder-only Transformers with no positional encodings, no layer norm, no bias, and no residual connections. Embeddings are fixed at initialization and do not change over the course of training. Transformers are initialized using μ\muP parameterization (Yang & Hu, 2021; Bordelon & Pehlevan, 2022). Specifically, for the model given in Section 3.2, we initialize the readout weights as 𝐰r∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈H)\mathbf{w}_{r}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{H}). We initialize all other weight matrices (𝐊,𝐐,𝐕,𝐖1\mathbf{K},\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{V},\mathbf{W}_{1}) with entries sampled iid from 𝒩⁡(0,H)\mathcal{N}(0,H). All activations are additionally scaled by a prefactor 1H\frac{1}{H} before passing to the next layer.

We use a learning rate of 1×10−​21\times 10^{-}2 and train our models using AdamW for 100 thousand iterations. To ensure the model sees every symbol about the same number of times, we set our batch size to be B​DBD, where BB is the number of branches and DD is the depth of the task. Unless otherwise stated, all evaluations are performed using 1024 samples.

  <if>h2 : (False → True) → p3</if>
  <if>h3 h4 : p1</if>
  <then>⊢ p1</then>
</state>
<tactic>exact h1</tactic>
<state id="5">
  <complete />
</state>
<success />

E.4 PHP split: example output

Example of an unsuccessful, non-terminating output on the PHP split. The model matches the ground truth for several thousand tokens before erroneously labeling a state with id 100, rather than 59. This appears to lead the model down an alternative computation path that does not terminate within the allotted max context length of 32 thousand tokens, despite the ground truth terminating well within this range. The output has been condensed slightly to improve readability.
